en: Their savage aspect appeared.
They mounted stallions from the herd,
Took single poles from the woods,
And became wildly excited.
Their strongest men, their lions,
Broad-chested and wide-breasted,
With long poles and pale clubs—
What well-formed wrestlers they were!
The Jediger had grown frenzied,
Bent that day on plundering the horde.
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
They meant to break the horde, seize plunder,
And unleash a great upheaval.
Darkening with grim resolve,
The Jediger entered the fray.
With a cry that deafened ears,
The Jediger entered the tumult.
Into an affliction with no remedy,
The Jediger entered the tumult.
They made their spears ready
And prepared their battle-axes.
They surged, roused to fury,
Saying to one another,
“Mount up, Jediger!”
Heroic Kiyaz thundered;
This was when he became inflamed.
“Break and take his horde!
Raid and take his horses!”
The slippery Kanchoro
Was rousing them at that moment.
When their khans issued a decree,
How could the people not be stirred?
If they refused the khan's word,
Would God not strike the populace?
The leaders of ten bustled,
The leaders of fifty strutted,
The leaders of a hundred ran,
And all the leaders of a thousand
Thus despaired of life.
Their heroes and brave men
Took battle-axes in hand.
Boasting as heroes and lions,
They simply swaggered in warlike pride.
They pounded the earth with a roar;
Their clamor split the sky.
The host filled broad Talas;
The dread and calamitous affair
Was not small but immense.
Clubmen formed the front,
Fighters stood at the flanks,
Swordsmen formed the front—
The formidable men stood at the flanks,
Spearmen formed the front;
Their lions stood behind,
Their renowned men in front,
Their champions at the flanks.
Their moon-crested standard became their banner,
And their shouts became a clamor.
Hill and valley were all uproar;
Everyone in the lowlands
Cried “Kiyaz!” as their battle cry.
On the hills were six hosts of horses;
The Jediger raised a shout
And raided them as they passed.
The countless black host rose as one
And reached the herd together.
In the mountains were ninety hosts of horses;
With piercing cries and clamor,
They raided them as they passed.
The countless black host rose as one
And reached the herd together.
The honored mighty warrior was dead.
The Jediger held a feast over
The warrior's countless black herds
And divided them by the measure of a whip.
Countless treasures and myriad goods—
The Jediger now swarmed the valley.
The Jediger filling Jeti-Özön
Feasted to the full
On the warrior-khan's wealth.
Every hero who had strength
Took a powerful, fleet horse;
Every wretched weakling
Took a shaggy, stormy colt.
The many Kyrgyz and Argyn of Talas
Now looked bitterly upon the pillage.
The Jediger cast catch-ropes
And separated out the Kyrgyz of Talas.
They inflicted unheard-of humiliation,
Extraordinary calamity and strife.
The Jediger swarmed in and took the livestock.
The foolish Jediger
Killed the men and took their lives.
The valley cried out and heaved;
Among the mingled Argyn and Kyrgyz,
The turmoil became devastation.
The teeming Jediger
Inflicted cruel suffering.
Saying, “This is for Chynkojo and Toltoy,”
They sacked them yet again.
The Jediger came in, sparing no soul,
Not one bay colt with a mane,
Not one lamb with a tail to provide meat,
Not one long-legged beast.
Of those able to wage war,
They spared no soul who could swing a club,
No hero who could lead a people,
No people capable of courage.
Among broad-rumped women with ornate hair pendants,
They spared no skilled young wife;
Among thimble-mouthed, camel-calf-eyed,
Rolling black-eyed girls
In crimson dresses with crescent waists,
They spared not one shimmering maiden.
They carried out a dreadful pillage,
And leaving them nothing at all,
They stood plundering everything.
At that time the Jediger
Went roaring and swaggering,
Their noses bulging like leather flasks.
“Our hostile warrior is dead,” they said;
“The accursed warrior has reached
The true place from which none returns.
Our grievous affliction and fetters are loosed;
God has granted this to us.
Now our season of fortune has come!”
They broke open the treasury;
They gorged themselves beyond measure on plunder.
A whole sable pelt
They slit down the middle
And put into their trouser cuffs.
Upon the warrior-khan's treasury,
The Jediger feasted to their fill
And lay there in a frenzy.
They took the most skilled of the women,
Chose and took the maidens from among the brides,
Took up their shameful work,
And loaded gold coins onto the camels.
Kanchoro, who had become ruler—
God had struck down the khan—
The Kyrgyz of Talas—
The Jediger swarmed utterly over them
And subject them to bloody pillage.
They stripped the Kyrgyz bare,
Standing there and plundering them.
They took livestock as spoil,
Entered without restraint and took lives.
They seized the yellow rolling ridges,
And plundered the people till they turned pale.
Of the Kyrgyz left lamenting,
They raided their mares from the hills,
And drove some of them away.
When an owner went to his mares,
They beat his brains out.
The Jediger wrought true slaughter
And thus raised their strife.
The dear people who had lived at peace—
They rummaged even through their bundles.
They dug a well in the place of honor
And trampled them down from above.
They slaughtered the leaders
And left them like an extinguished fire.
Then the Jediger
Were sated without a care
With packhorses and thoroughbreds.
The Jediger of Jeti-Özön
All mounted up in high spirits.
They overran the villages
And slaughtered the wise heroes.
They made the bustling Kyrgyz
Like a fire put out.
The great people fled in panic
And met with ruinous calamity.
The great black host of Jediger
Rose as one with a thunder;
They left none at the root
And made them like a fire put out.
Now they brought another calamity;
They exacted together the vengeance
Not only of Toltoy but of Bagysh.
Not long after that—
A garden of plane trees all around,
A golden throne at its center—
When the mighty warrior died, Külchoro
Could no longer make himself known.
Our fortune had been bound fast;
A deep pit had been dug.
Both hands had been bound,
An iron net spread wide,
And vast misery set boiling.
Fortune fled and our backs were broken;
Courage fled and our spirits broke.
A dark calamity struck us:
Semetey was not dead, yet the people died;
All the great Kyrgyz nation died,
And the ancient joyous way of life died.
The wide world became narrow;
The open plain became a prison.
Our poor heads that never drank kumys
Longed for muddy water;
Our poor heads that never drank spirits
Longed for sour water.
Bereft of the towering lion,
The many Kyrgyz and Argyn in Talas—
The black multitude sobbed and wept,
All the other people wept together,
As they endured this butchery.
The women wailed, the people wept,
The multitude stood in turmoil;
The throng that once strode proudly
Now stood there in this state,
Become like witless cattle.
Thus was the great host struck down;
They cried, “My bloodthirsty lord, do not die!”
How could his honor be hidden?
The Argyn people’s hearts sank;
Though they stood there lamenting,
Though they grieved and wailed,
The valiant gray wolf could not be found.
Let us leave that matter there,
And begin with this calamity:
No human should suffer such violence,
No such humiliation exists in all the world.
There, at the dark eye of the spring,
Beside the very straight plane tree,
Below Tört-Kül,
In the garden planted by noble Manas,
On the plain facing Bart-Köl,
Along the Üch-Koshoy,
Within the walled enclosure,
Stood Aychürök’s white palace.
Its strength was of this kind:
Stones were heaped into a mountain,
Cliffs were raised all around it;
Spears struck it and were blunted,
Enemies despaired of taking it.
And at the palace entrance—
Behold all its wonders—
Fire was drawn from six channels of earth;
That luckless palace, matchless in beauty,
Had been fashioned by magic—
Behold the wonder of its making.
Sixty matching black camels
Could not reach it against a raging foe;
None who fought there left alive.
Going farther on,
Fifteen mares had foaled tigers there;
No person had ever approached
A palace of such design,
No enemy approaching it had prevailed.
Those who heard its fame marveled;
Those who saw it wandered dazed.
The white palace stood in a renowned place,
Built at the poor woman’s command;
Such was its strength.
